utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Now, we had thought this morning at the outset to hear submissions on the two matters that I mentioned last evening, so that we can clear those out of the way. It should only be a very brief interlude. You, I believe, Mr. Petrovic, wanted to advance briefly some oral submissions concerning the timetable for the availability of the statements of expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, that is correct. You surely know that at the Pre-Trial Conference which was held on the 15th of December, the Pre-Trial Judge ordered the OTP to provide, by the 31st of December last year, or rather, to disclose all the statements made by expert witnesses. There are total four of them. So that was the order given on the 15th of September [as interpreted]. Just about at the end of last year, the OTP this to be postponed, stating certain reasons that I would like briefly to review. The OTP evoked a conversation that was conducted in September last year in the office of Professor Harhoff, where it was discussed the procedure for disclosure of expert reports. In that discussion, a principle -- an agreement in principle was reached for the expert witness of Dr. Allcock, who already appeared in this Court, to be disclosed within three weeks, whereas for the other statements by expert witnesses to be disclosed within four weeks, each before their making testimony. That was an informal conversation in the offices of Mr. Harhoff, and that is the first important circumstance. And the second important circumstance is that this was not a Status Conference in compliance with Rule 65 ter. So the second important circumstance is that on the 25th of July last year, all of a sudden a trial was set within six weeks, and it was supposed to commence on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Petrovic. The interpreter is not able to keep up with your very fluid delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to you, Your Honour, and to the interpreters. So this conference was conducted under the circumstances when it was anticipated that within a very short time, that is, six or seven weeks, for the trial to begin. Mrs. Somers and her team, as well as we, were surprised with such short notice for the trial to begin. We both had problems. The case was only halfway through. The expert witnesses were practically not identified at the time. Our problems also existed, and they were very big, but I will not go into that now. So under such circumstances, as a token of understanding and compromise, we accepted the date, and that is the 9th of October, and to reduce these deadlines, as has been stated in the OTP submission in December last year. That was our concession under such circumstances, which was very difficult, both for Mrs. Somers and for us, and she will probably confirm that. However, since then, four months have elapsed, and the OTP had enough time and they were very much involved in the preparations, so the situation became different. The trial, which was set for the 9th of October, was postponed for the 10th of December, and that is a full three months to work. So everything that we had agreed earlier simply lost any meaning or reasons, because the trial had been postponed and enough time was given for all these things to be settled in a manner that is prescribed by the Rules. Therefore, at the time, we thought that the trial would begin on the 9th of October, that it was going to last for about 10 or 12 weeks, and under such circumstances, naturally, no deadline before the end of the last year was meaningless. The situation with the rest of Vladimir Kovacevic changed the situation entirely. Therefore, whatever we agreed at the time cannot be something that we can rely upon any further. The deadline put forward by the Pre-Trial Judge on the 15th of December was quite reasonable. The 31st of December was the date, which made it possible, primarily for the Defence, to provide, in time and in a proper manner, its own views and analyses of the expert findings. We again made a concession and reached a compromise, at the request and the telephone question by our colleague, Nick Kaufman which he conducted on the 23rd or 24th December last year, and at his request, whether we agreed to make a concession and extend the deadline for a few days, we again were cooperative and we said that the 12th of January was the date when the session was going to begin, so let us shift this date of 31st of December to the 12th of January. Since then, more than two weeks have elapsed and we still have not received the expert findings. There was no decision made on that matter. Therefore, our view, and since today is the 27th of January, and that is 27 days after the deadline, which is still valid, and made by the Pre-Trial Judge, we kindly request that there was no further postponement allowed by you, and that we treat this date or this deadline as expired and that everything that relates to the expert findings be given to the Defence. Why do we think so? You certainly know how the Defence team is composed. My learned colleague Rodic and I constitute the team defence, plus one investigator and one case manager. So we are here, we don't have any logistics support here, we don't have people with whom we can consult, we don't have any reference material here with which we can adequately contest what is probably going to be contained in the expert statements. Every day is of crucial importance for us, in order to enable us to be effective in providing responses, in doing cross-examination of expert witnesses who are going to appear here. So every day is of crucial importance. Therefore, I kindly ask, and I do appreciate the problems of the OTP, but please believe me that we are also facing much bigger problems, particularly in regard with the lack of the logistic. Mrs. Somers has a very well-trained team of lawyers and she has available all other means. Whenever she needs an expert from any given area, this expert appears in this Court and contributes to the effective work of the OTP. We are alone, however. So in this situation, this would at least be some alleviation of the problems that we are facing if we could get these materials as soon as possible. In this regard, there's another important matter, and that is the question of the translation of expert statements. In many Trial Chambers of this Tribunal, the moment when the expert statement is considered valid and in force, is once it is submitted in the language which it has been made, plus in the translation into B/C/S. Why do I say that? In many Chambers, this has been upheld because the characteristics of an expert statement are in many aspects coinciding with the statement given by the witness under Rule 66, and it is considered to be valid and disclosed to the other side only once it has been translated into the language that the accused understands. We may interpret and analyse an expert witness's statement; however, we believe that our client and the defendant is also entitled to learn what is contained in those reports. However, he's unable to do that unless these documents are translated into B/C/S. So there's another additional problem that we are facing. Let me just remind you that the last report made by Mr. Pringle, and that is the person who should appear before this Court, I believe, on Thursday and Friday, on the 22nd of December, it was submitted in an English version. We worked on it. Unfortunately, only on the 16th of January this statement was submitted in B/C/S. Only then was the accused in a position to see what is contained in that material, without us interpreting or retelling to him what stands in the report. Another important thing that we should mention and which sheds additional light to what I have just said is the following fact: In most cases, at least in our experience, the issue of the disclosure of expert statement is something that takes place in a pre-trial stage, in the early stages of the pre-trial stage. Expert statements waiting to reach the trial have already been disclosed. Rule 94 bis provides 30 days for giving a response to the expert witness statement, which is something of a formal nature. Substantially, these statements have already been in the hands of the Defence for months in a row. So we are very much into this trial, whereas the key reports concerning command and control, concerning the use of artillery units, et cetera, we only know the names of the people who are going to appear here as expert witnesses. Nothing other than that. Can you imagine just a witness -- expert witness statements concerning artillery issue, how important and serious this is going to be? So here in The Hague, while the trial is in progress, we have to analyse and file proper responses. So I kindly ask this Chamber to order all expert statements to be disclosed as soon as possible, in order to make it possible for us to prepare the defence of Mr. Pavle Strugar in a proper manner. Furthermore, there is another issue that I wish to bring up, which is not directly related to what I've discussed up to now, but may as well affect it in one way or another. What we want to know, Your Honours, and this is something we have not heard from you so far, is about the pace at which this case will proceed, how evidence will continue before the Chamber, and whether the OTP may be planning any breaks in its case, long breaks, or brief ones, what the deadline will be for 98 bis -- for the 98 bis evidence, how much time there will be between the end of the Prosecutor's case and the 98 bis, and before the Defence case begins. All these things would be very useful to know for the Defence in planning its case, as well as its response to the Prosecutor's case. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I'm sorry if I've taken up a little more time than you originally planned for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. First of all, I would want the Chamber to understand -- to know something about the meeting to which Mr. Petrovic was referring, and it goes right to the heart of the relationship between and among the Chamber, the legal officer, and the parties. The only types of meetings that legal officers are authorised to hold are in connection with 65 ter. There's no such thing in this sense as an informal meeting. There was a recorded 65 ter conference on the 19th of September with Mr. Petrovic and members of the Office of the Prosecutor, as well as Registry officials and the legal officers, from both teams -- I'm sorry. From -- it was a team, 1 Pre-Trial Conference at that point. At that time -- and I don't have the transcript in front of me, but Mr. Harhoff, the legal officer, requested that before Mr. Petrovic return to Belgrade we meet again in his office as a follow-up to discuss any new items and I -- if it -- was not aware that there was going to be a need for a transcript. But we in fact did meet at -- I believe it was 9.00 in the morning on 24 September and my notes reflect 65 ter, and I have the individuals present. And it was in every sense a follow-up to discuss issues that were outstanding, among them the issue of experts. And it was made clear at that time that the deadlines that we were looking at to some degree varied with what were in the current state of the Rules. But my notes very clearly reflect and I believe I may have overestimated my response that was filed on 24 December, I was on the phone with Mr. Kaufmann, who was on the phone with Belgrade, I was in the US and it was a three-way call in that sense, where my notes reflect for Dr. Allcock two weeks would have been sufficient in any language, two weeks, and then for the military experts three weeks. But the date was always to be set by us with an understanding that it had to be within time limits. The reason that's an important factor, beside the fact that this is what was -- what we left that office with and what we communicated to our people to communicate to the persons who were working on the reports is that we have to make the same assumption that when we speak to legal officers, that they have -- they are speaking on behalf of their Chambers. And we have at all times had that understanding. I believe that when at the Pre-Trial Conference on the 15th of December, this was the first time there was ever a discussion or an order concerning end of the year. I mean, this simply had not been part of it. We in no way contest what the current Rule grants to the Chamber or the pre-trial Chamber on deadlines. No one is arguing that. We're just saying we rely on what we're told and what's agreed to. And a change like that is a sea change, where literally on the eve of holidays and on the threshold of trial, trial commencing the 16th, deadlines, which are very important deadlines and which we have to honour, unless we can indicate that they should be amended, are changed. I mean, it's the question of -- on whose word do we rely, and we believe there may have been some miscommunication, because certainly the end of the year issue was the first -- was first raised on the 15th of December. Our request, under all circumstances, to return to the original agreement which was made with full input of Defence counsel, and we'd ask the Chamber to endorse it, understanding the pressures on both sides. And Mr. Petrovic speaks very much the truth about that, that not only were there changes in trial schedules, but dramatic changes in the thrust of inquiry by experts, given -- and some aspects, not in entirety - be given the reduction of 15 counts to a very generalised Dubrovnik area, to specifically Old Town, which had its own unique aspects. But we also found ourselves having to scramble very quickly to get witnesses in earlier than the original dates that were contemplated, which my transcripts from a conference concerning Mr. Kovacevic indicate we were talking 8th or 9th of February as a starting date. Whereas this is not something that this Chamber has any responsibility for, I think it only fair that it know the very convoluted history of setting, resetting, joint trial, severed trial, and what it does to persons unrelated at the Tribunal working on behalf of a request by the Office of the Prosecution and perhaps by the Defence. So there has been at no time any taking lightly of deadlines or considerations. We try to operate under what is reasonable and we have to assume that when we have been instructed, and it's in -- not just in consultation with, but in reduction of time. The Defence had its own specific views and it agreed to certain things, that we have to be able to rely on it. If there is a change in this we'd ask that we are at least able to produce to the Chamber, within a reasonable time, and I can indicate now that the -- we're in the completion phase, but understandably, we want to make sure that you get the product that will be of assistance to you. Again, my concern really goes more toward the timing of certain orders. I set that forth in my response, in my request for a stay. This is -- we ask not that this be taken as any form of criticism, but simply that all parties have to be singing from the same hymn sheet. And I'm afraid in this instance, given a number of factors, all which are true, I think Mr. Petrovic speaks correctly, except that this is not a David versus Goliath. The Prosecution doesn't have anything unlimited including attorneys or access to experts. What is very interesting as I recall the other day a comment was made about the honour and privilege it is to serve -- or to testify before the Tribunal. Perhaps the one time where that is not necessarily the case is in getting experts. It is very difficult to find people who can line up precisely with issues, people do not actually wait to be asked. I have to take a little issue about enthusiasm level. And we are always very gratified when we are able to retain persons who we think are the very best suited, under all circumstances, but they are going to be the persons who are also busy with their own schedules. Because we communicated other deadlines, I would not want to see the experts punished or the OTP, or in fact if the Defence runs into a problem. We can understand how that would work. Just so that it was -- that I can make it clear to the Chamber that there was a very different set of marching orders when we left that conference on the 24th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What about when you left the hearing before the Pre-Trial Judge in mid-December?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that very well. We also indicated that the suggestion that was made by the Defence that years in advance. That is simply not part of this -- the procedure of the Tribunal. And I wanted to call to the Chamber's attention the -- how it has -- in the interests, I presume, of time, or perhaps other factors, how the Rules change. It had always been under the old 94 bis and I'll simply take a moment to read from the 19 -- sorry, the 2001 draft, which although no longer governs, gives an idea that the representation about reports being made years, light years in advance, is simply not the case. It has never been the case, and I think I can think of one case in the Tribunal where in the abstract a court can be filed which it is not tailored to the Defence's, or the defence of the Defence, as usually is set forth for the first time in the pre-trial brief. But the old 94 bis, which is only recently amended, put a time limit of, "full statement of any expert witness called by a party shall be disclosed to the party as soon as possible and shall be filed not less than 21 days prior to the date on which the expert is expected to testify, then for the 14 day limit." The point being that it was, of course, the party calling that decided the order of the witness and within a given period of time would provide the report. It has no -- but today's Rule puts it squarely in the hands of the Trial Chamber or the Pre-Trial Judge. Again, the Pre-Trial Judge's order came only on the 15th of December, whereas the Pre-Trial Judge's legal officers hand an order to us had come on the 19th - sorry - the 24th of September. Even putting that aside, looking at the reality of what is at issue in terms of translations, that is not correct. The translation of an expert statement is not addressed in 94 bis. I would take issue with Mr. Petrovic's assertion that this is an institutional practice. Where possible, it's done. But there are reasons why Defence teams have to have an English-speaking member of the team. And in fact this goes for anything, other than 66(A) -- the 66 Rule has a requirement that statements filed be in the language of the accused, or a language the accused understands. That is not found in any of the 94 provisions. Having said that, it will probably be simpler because the particular individuals whose statements are outstanding and are being completed are from the former Yugoslavia and it should be less cumbersome certainly to provide more quickly. But the date of filing is the date is goes in in a language that's acceptable to the Tribunal, which is either French or English. Documents can only be filed in one of those two languages. And filing is the trigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That didn't deal with the issue that was in my mind. No doubt I failed to make it clear. You have stressed that you have planned things from September on the basis of understandings then in place. They were well known to the Judge on the 15th of December, and he required the delivery of all statements by the end of the month, effectively. And it is now a further month, and they have not been delivered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the -- if Your Honour is referring to -- the Chamber to legal officers' comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the order of the Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But that -- I would have to link that order to everything that was said before, because we operated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. Why? You've had that in place, and then the Judge made an order, giving a date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Because we had indicated to the persons who were writing the earlier, and it was not possible to make the change at the time. It was already 15 December. The team -- it was one week of trial expedited. No one contemplated this case starting before the end of the year. And the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That doesn't help me, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What I'm trying to give you is the absolute truth of how we rely on what is said. Excuse me. We'd have to file a motion explaining the reasons. And that is what I did. I tried to make it clear that there was no wilful noncompliance but that based on factors which we thought were reasonable and good cause, we had had a timetable that varied, and it was our understanding, it was our understanding, that it would be a 30-day time limit, from what I believe the Senior Legal Officer from Chamber 2 mentioned, but that we would set the date and 30 days from the date would be when we'd have to have -- 30 days in advance of the date. Which is a reasonable interpretation. When the Chamber ordered on the 15, we were effectively caught short. We were simply unable at that time, given the history of it, to produce on that timetable. It was simply a different one. Again, if we could live life over again and have a firm, you must have it by such-and-such, then we can plan it that way. It simply did not work out. There was not any conscious effort to avoid that. But again, we had no reason to believe that we would be asked to provide it at that point in time, given our understanding of 30 days, but at the 65 ter conference in December, again, no actual deadline set, just 30 days. There's a world of difference between 30 days before and then a fixed deadline. And if the two are to be linked, then in the same way I would not ask my colleagues for something that would be -- that would completely derail their trial preparation, I would expect not to have that also put on us. And if in fact there was a failure at the December conference on any party's part, perhaps we both could have said, Okay, if you're saying 30 days, what do you mean? But a definite time would need to be arranged sufficiently in advance. And again, I think that it may have been a bit of a lesson for all that things that are left too vague end up in motions like this. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't see any vagueness about the obligation that was placed on the Prosecution, nor do I see any vagueness about the fact that the Prosecution is now effectively a month out of time. Can you tell me what it is that you now propose in terms of our timetable?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. I would ask Your Honour, because the issue -- because the documents are so substantially close to completion, but because they are -- there are language issues, that we be given -- well, I had anticipated calling these individuals at the end of the trial, toward the very end of the trial, and I don't know how we identify the end of the trial right now, but if it is more mid-March, then I would ask for approximately ten more days to make sure that at least linguistically everything is okay and that our particular military analysis person is able to be satisfied that the inquiries on our part have been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How many reports have we?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Considering?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Correct. The and the Chamber has already the other two they've been in. And they are -- we've already heard Dr. Allcock, he came up second witness, and then General Pringle is scheduled for Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And are these two reports at an equal stage of preparation or is one further ahead than the other?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Equal. I would say they're equal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You want ten further days?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, can we, for a moment, the submissions of Mr. Petrovic and your own just then have opened the horizons on future timetable. Can you indicate to the Chamber the anticipation you have for the end of the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I was trying to estimate from my reading of the transcript in the Pre-Trial Conference that if the Defence got 60 per cent of the Prosecution time - am I correct on that approximation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't work on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, that's how we planned it. It is clear that that is not going to work, and on those calculations, if I recall correctly, I think His Honour Judge Orie thought maybe 5th of March. I don't think that was ever realistic. And that also factored in issues with the accused's health and the inability to sit, let's say, full days all week. It looks to me that we're looking at the middle to the end of March, if Defence continues -- if we cannot take two witnesses a day, and in some instances three witnesses a day, and after the 65 -- the decisions on both video and 92 bis, we're going to -- it's going to be pretty much a live presentation, literally. I think the only 92 bis ones were the decedents, if I'm not wrong. So that is going to take perhaps a bit more time, and I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest that there is a difference between some of the witnesses we've been dealing with and some of those that are to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There has been reason why the Chamber has been prepared to allow considerable liberty of time to the Defence with some of the witnesses that we've been dealing with. But many of those to come are not of that significance and relevance, not of the same importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And for that reason, we would expect that the course of cross-examination for them will be proportionately much shorter than has been for some of the witnesses until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But having said that -- and I agree with Your Honour, because many are crime base. But some are fact witnesses who are also from ECMM. The former accused will also be testifying. And that is -- those are lengthy, and I expect cross-examination to be very lengthy and relatively document-heavy. So I really could not in all honesty foresee much -- I would estimate between the middle and the end of March as an optimistic finish, if we stay with reasonable cross-examination. I mean, just having practiced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you anticipating the need for any breaks in the course of your case?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You mean before we finish, Your Honour? I have never had a break in my case before we finished. If the Chamber is proposing something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was raised not by me. It was raised by Mr. Petrovic. And I thought maybe you knew something I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, but I mean, clearly, all of us suffer this from the same pace. No one has it any easier, and we appreciate the Chamber and all of our colleagues are under it. I'm encouraged by all my colleagues who say yes. In honesty, did we anticipate anything? We did not. We anticipated going forward. What we're finding is because of having to re-call witnesses whose testimony is left perhaps in midstream during cross-examination, our schedule which we present to the Defence changes more often than we want. It's hard on them. It's hard on us. VWU finds itself, for example, today I was asked about a witness who is scheduled to testify this week, who's here, and it is very unlikely that we will be able to get to this person's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Especially given the time we're talking this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I know but I think the issue is terribly important to resolve because there's the theory and there's the reality, and the reality is we deal with issues that arise like this and also during cross-examination things have been coming up. And admittedly on one point we had to take more time in direct than was anticipated. I think that is very much the exception. But I would have to estimate realistically, end of March, and no, I don't see any breaks, unless the Chamber is inclined to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not our desire to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But I feared from what was said by Mr. Petrovic that there had been some discussion between you about a break for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I just want to also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But we can leave that aside.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. I wish we could. I regret we can't. But as to a level playing field, we all operate under the same disabilities. Very few extra abilities. And in consequence, I would ask that my application for extension be granted. I think that given all circumstances, again if perhaps clarity had been more -- or if there had been no room for raising these issues, then it might have been easier, but I want to assure the Chamber of our good faith and I'm sure the Defence, who has today indicated and acknowledged that there was a different line of discussion, I'm grateful for that. We are trying to move things along as fast as we can and present the very best and most brief picture we can to this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, was there any important matter that you needed to respond with? You were half to your feet at one point there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I merely wish to say, although the best part of what my learned friend spoke about was not entirely clear to me, I knew what she was saying, but I didn't know where she was getting at, I don't think the essence of our complaint has been addressed. The trial was due to commence on the 9th of October initially. And secondly, another thing which we would like you to bear in mind, the trial was scheduled initially for the 25th of July last year. It has been six months since, a full six months, and we still don't have these reports. The Pre-Trial Judge is someone who is supposed to make a decision as to when disclosure would occur. There is no 30-day limit. It's only a formal limit, pursuant to Rule 94 bis (B). Rule 94 bis (A) is entirely clear, the situation from October and the situation from December are two entirely different situations. We were hoping to receive these reports by the 31st of December, so that in the remaining few days before January's hearing we could work on those and work to achieve whatever we could. However, we can only do this work in Belgrade or Podgorica. Bearing in mind the fact that today is the 27th of January, the problem we are facing now is when will this happen? Will there be a deadline again, a five- ten- or 15-day deadline? That's one thing. And the other is, and this is something we've talked about already, even for the sake of basic information, even if we had the statement in the language in which it was provided, even if was Slovene, none of us speak Slovene, but maybe just to inform ourselves to see how subjects are broached -- approached, to see what the attachments are, to see how the issues are treated in these reports. We've talked about this many times. We understand your problems, but please let us have the statements in a language which may not be the official language of the Tribunal and may not be the language of the accused. But we've never even received that. The only conclusion we can draw from that is that we are now compelled to ask you for a break in the proceedings that would enable us to analyse these reports, to consult our own experts, and to prepare our cross-examinations. This could be one of the consequences of what has been going on here, and I would not like to now take up any more of your time, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. We are of the view that any further statements of experts upon which the Prosecution wishes to rely, and we understand that there are two in issue, should be filed by Tuesday of next week, which is seven days, not ten; and if not filed by then, the prospect that that evidence would not be able to be admitted is one that must be faced.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will convey this to the MAT immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, your concern that you may then find that you are without adequate time for preparation is something that I think neither you nor the Chamber can assess at the present time. It's too early yet. But if you can receive the statements, and from what has been said, you'll receive them in both English and B/C/S by next Tuesday, the question can then be considered. If you find that you are in real difficulty, we'll have to assess the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I cannot guarantee the B/C/S on both by next Tuesday. The English, absolutely, the filed copy, yes, and we'll endeavour to ask CLSS if they can expedite, but that will again -- I cannot guarantee that. I'll certainly have the English file copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, again we are facing a situation where your decision, which in itself represents quite a concession to the OTP, is being challenged. We all know how these cases are treated at this Tribunal, and we all know that this should be resolved. So please do not allow any further challenges to be made to your decision which you have made. We appeal to this Trial Chamber to make sure that this decision is implemented in the way as decided by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I had understood that part of the reason for this delay was to complete translation. I may have misunderstood what Ms. Somers was saying. We cannot specifically order that a statement be provided in B/S/C. We can order that a statement be filed. That we do, and that must be done by next Tuesday. I would expect that every effort be made by the Prosecution to provide to you the same statement translated into B/S/C at the same time. If that is not the case, and there is any further delay, that will certainly be a factor which this Chamber must take into account if you are obliged to come later and ask for some further time to enable you to prepare in response to the statement. And we hope that can be avoided by the availability of the translation, as well as the English or French-language version, by next Tuesday. Now, I think that is the end of that matter. There remains the other matter, the question of the relevance and admissibility of some of the evidence of the expert contemplated for the end of this week, General Pringle. I see we have now received a written response, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was filed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid you saw the Chamber receive it just then. We were not aware of it until just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My apologies. I don't know the distribution process, but what we'll do in the future is try to get a courtesy copy. Apparently it is an issue with distribution. I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there anything that you would add, briefly, to these written submissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think these submissions, Your Honour, stand very much on their own. This clearly goes to very much the heart of command and control issues, 7(3) and 7(1) in this instance, where 7(3) has led to 7(1), and I think the Chamber will find that the fact that this is a British general is irrelevant, that what is important is the principles that are espoused in modern armies and in modern forces and will find this evidence both relevant and exceptionally helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will appreciate, Ms. Somers, that it will be a matter of evidence whether any principles that are the subject of evidence of this nature are principles that had a place in the army of the accused man at the relevant time. There is no just general principle, that what is a good principle for the management of armies is a principle that was in place in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Completely, Your Honour, and that is addressed in the submission of General Pringle, who is familiar with the particular forces, or at least the rules and regulations of the forces. I believe that the issues are not appropriately addressed by the Defence in exclusion. I mean, these are matters that would go to weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, is there anything that you need to add to your written submission on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have much to add. The essence of our objection is, as for the first part, related to the person, personality of the expert witness, which you will rule upon; as for the other matter, it is something to do with evidence. The question of relevance is the previous question that needs to be discussed. The first question that needs to be discussed. Why? Because here we are dealing with norms and principles that were simply not in place in the JNA at the relevant time. This is completely extraneous to the JNA. Principles applied in the British army and the principles applied in the JNA are two completely heterogeneous principles. These two armies were the result of two completely different societies. You have the communist system and recruits, on the one hand, and a professional British army on the other. There are no similarities whatsoever. Mr. Pringle uses two documents, a mere two documents, for his analysis, which I assume he obtained from the OTP. And basing his conclusions on these two documents, he's trying to establish purported similarities between the British army and the JNA, whereas in reality, these two couldn't be further apart. These are two distant sides of the same coin, at best. It is up to you to decide whether you want to hear this evidence on Thursday and Friday, but how, I wonder, can one compare the JNA to the British Army. I think, frankly, he's facing an impossible task. However, if the OTP believe that this will be a useful testimony, useful evidence for their case, even with all the resources that are being expended here, we have no other choice but to accept their idea. However, we believe it would be a very time-saving move to avoid this evidence being provided live in Court, as proposed in our motion. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. We having just received the written response, we will need to give some consideration to it before giving a decision. Now, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will -- if the Chamber permits us to move at this point, Mr. Weiner will be leading the evidence of the next Prosecution witness, Mr. Ivo Grbic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which name is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Grbic, G-r-b-i-c, Ivo. May I ask the Chamber's indulgence to allow me to leave for a few moments, and I'll return. I will return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I just wanted to follow up on some of what was discussed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're leaving us in the hands of Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You are in good hands and I wanted to introduce you to another member of the OTP, Ms. Prashanthi Mahindaratne, who is a trial lawyer as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weiner. Could the witness be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are informed that there is a temporary difficulty with the witness coming into Court. What we would propose, then, is to have the first morning break now, earlier than usual, but it will give an opportunity for the witness to be ready to return. And our break will be for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would take the affirmation, Mr. Grbic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you state your name, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: My name is Ivo Grbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you live?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I now live in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How old are you, and could you tell us your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th October, 1931.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That makes you 72 years old?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I just turned 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How are you employed?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I am a retired painter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say "painter," you mean an artist?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in addition to being an artist, did you also teach or serve as a professor in art school?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Not any more. But for many years, I taught at the school of applied arts in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And just to be brief, sir: Your art works have been exhibited in Europe, Asia, and South America?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, where do you live in Dubrovnik? Where exactly in the Old Town of Dubrovnik? What's the address?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Almost at the geometrical centre of town, and the address is Od Puca number 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When did you move to Od Puca 16?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: When I got separated in Zagreb, I went to live with my parents in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In what year?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I came to Dubrovnik in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long had your parents been living there, in that particular home?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: My parents had been living there since 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please describe that building for the Court, Od Puca 16.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: This palace was built after a tremendous earthquake in 1667. It bore all the characteristics of a Baroque palace, particularly specific features were three balconies, with the railings of wrought iron, made in the shapes of flowers, and that's a unique feature in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, where did you live? Where did your family live within the building?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We lived on the second floor, but we also used the entire loft.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's the attic? When you say "loft," you mean an attic, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, that was not a residential space. There were installations there, and a very old Baroque kitchen was housed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Who else lived in the building?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Another family lived on the first floor. The mother of the daughter was named Goja, who married Mr. Lucic, and they are the only two tenants there now, the family Lucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let us move to October 1991, October 1st. Were you living there on October 1st?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did something happen around 7.00 a.m. on October 1st, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Something very important happened, and that is that two aircraft targeted the TV tower on the top of the Srdj hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And after that, what happened to the TV tower after it was targeted?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It was pierced and rendered unusable; besides, something else happened, which was for us completely new. There was no electric power or water supply in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any type of blockade at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Certainly. We were blockaded, particularly from the side of the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, during this situation where you were blockaded and there was a loss of power and water, what did you do to obtain water?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We used water tanks, the biggest ones were in the Franciscan and Dominican monasteries, and some private houses had their own water cisterns on the ground floor. And we shared the water among ourselves in a very careful and rational manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there any means of water collection that your family and some of the other families used, any other means than going to wells?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Only on or around the 1st of November, the rain fell, and only then we started using some auxiliary instruments in order to collect this rainwater. For example, I cut off the top of a plastic bottle and tied it to the drain pipe from the roof, and installed a pipe into the house, where we collected in water in a larger vessel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's continue in October of 1991. Was the Old Town shelled during that month?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Approximately when in the month was it shelled?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: In late October, sometime around 23rd or the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, please tell the Judges: What were you doing when this happened, when the shelling happened?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I was in my street, which is called Od Puca. We were strolling -- my sister and I were strolling on the street. At the end of the street, to the west, there was a shoe store. My sister, as women do more often than men, stopped to look at the shop window, and I was standing by her side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did something happen?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Then something that nobody had expected took place. Behind our backs, from the south, we felt a very strong explosion. Pieces of roof tiles, stones, and also shrapnel, poured over the entire block of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We then ran back to our house. That was about -- the distance was about 70 metres. My sister went into the house, and very close to our house, in Djordjiceva Street, I saw a flaring object, and that was a shrapnel, or a piece of a shell. And I took it in my hand while it was still warm. At that point, it seemed to be like a wonderful souvenir to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you -- you went to the house?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I immediately went to the house, but no one believed that something terrible would happen later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do while in the house?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I went to the window facing west in our flat, and I saw a hole in the roof of the Rupe Museum, because I have a very good view of this roof from my window. That is to the south of our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you remain at that window in your home?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I stayed there for a short while, because I was stunned that somebody would dare to shell this gorgeous, wonderful town, which was under the UNESCO protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did something happen while you stayed at the window?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Then I went to the east side of our house, to the window facing east. Then I heard an unusual sound, as if a bird was flying, making a noise, hrrr [phoen]. I ran back to the room and lay down on the floor, and at that moment, I heard another powerful explosion nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you return to the window and see what had happened?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I saw smoke from on the same side of the Od Puca Street, no more than 20 metres from the window. I saw smoke. Then later, when we went outside, we noticed that the loft of the house owned by Mr. Pecar was -- had been hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the damage to the Pecar home?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: There were two skylight windows on the roof of the house. Underneath there was a kitchen. The shell blew up all that. Luckily, the family was not in the kitchen at the time but in the floor below. So they were spared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What is the distance of the Pecar home from your home?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: From the corner of my house, there is about 19 or 20 metres from the Pecar house. They are very close to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, the damage to the Pecar house and the damage to the Rupe Museum, did that exist prior to your hearing the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No. Those were the first shells that were registered to land within the walls of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on the following day, sir, did you have a chance to walk around the town, the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We were all shocked, and all citizens walked around the town in order to see whether there was any other damage caused. We reached the Boskovica Street, which was named after one of the greatest minds of this world, Rudjer Boskovic. Another shell landed on this street as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did that shell cause any damage that you observed?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It caused substantial damage on the both sides of the street. On the right-hand side of the street, there was, and there still is, the third oldest synagogue in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what damage was caused to the synagogue?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: All the windows were broken, the window frames, the cornerstones, because a shell can cause damage on anything that it hits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other buildings that were damaged?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: This took place in October, what I have just been describing, and I eyewitnessed all these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I understand that. But in October, did you see any other buildings that were damaged in the vicinity of the synagogue?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. As I said, when a shell lands, it causes damage to the nearby houses. In this case, it was a synagogue. However, I don't know who the owners of those houses were in order to give you their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you see any other damage caused by the shelling in October?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were any boats, vehicles, any sort of moving objects damaged?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought you were referring just to buildings. Yes, certainly. To the north, behind the city walls, there is a sort of parking lot, and from my house I could see that very thick and black smoke was coming up from that area. Why? Because many cars had been hit, and they were burnt as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said behind the city walls. Where do you mean? Is this within the Old Town or outside?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No, no. Outside the Old Town, to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how far is this parking area from the walls of the Old Town, the northern walls?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It was adjacent to the walls. That used to be a football playground, but after that, they coated it with asphalt and turned it into a parking area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, on that date, while you were walking with your sister, or any other date in October, did you see any artillery or mortars within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any Croatian troops within the Old Town in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any troops, soldiers, or anyone else firing from the walls of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, did you ever see any outgoing fire of any kind in October of 1991 from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No. That was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: We just talked about artillery and mortars. Are you somewhat familiar with artillery and mortars?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, had you ever served in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When did you serve?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: In 1958, after I had graduated, until 1959, so one year in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in what type of unit were you assigned in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I spent three months in an artillery unit in the town of Cuprija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, since that training in 1958 and 1959 and your service during that year, had you received any subsequent training, or had you done any subsequent service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Not any more, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to November of 1991. Were you still living on Od Puca Street?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Chamber: Was the Old Town shelled during the month of November?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I know that on Sunday, the 10th, Monday, the 11th, and Tuesday, the 12th, there were three consecutive days of shelling. Shells were whirring past and over the town. We never left our homes. We were afraid of going on. On Tuesday, the 12th, it was particularly horrifying, and my sister almost broke down. I told her to fill her ears with cotton so she would hear less of the explosions. On that particular Tuesday, the firing went on for ten straight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you observe any damage that had occurred as a result of that shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It was only after we were able to leave our homes, because on Wednesday, the 13th, there was some kind of a lull, a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you left your home, did you observe any damage?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I went out with my sister, and I lived with my old mother, who was 87 years old. So I used to go strolling with my sister. We went outside the city walls, to an area west of the town, which is known as Pile. There was some kind of a clearing there, an open area, from which you could survey damage to the Bokar tower, which is part of the town walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is that in the western section of the Old Town walls, the Bokar tower?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That's correct. This is the most prominent, the most protruding part of the town wall in the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you notice any other damage after that shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We noticed more similar damage to the stones supporting the Lovrinac Fort.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about, sir, within the Old Town, did you notice any damage to the -- anything that's movable: Trucks, vehicles, vessels, or boats?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We know that when Dubrovnik was under siege, not the smallest vessel was allowed to leave the harbour. There were no trucks in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about -- was there any damage to any of those vehicles or boats or vessels after the November shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: There was severe damage to boats, private boats, big and small. This damage occurred in the town harbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, was there any sniping, shots by rifles, into the Old Town during the month of November? Please tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, this was the case. I personally witnessed individual instances of sniping by soldiers who were within our eyesight. They were standing on top of Svijetlje [phoen] Rocks, which is between Srdj and Zarkovica. We could see them silhouetted against the white stone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us about the incidents of sniping into the Old Town, or rifle fire into the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Again, I was out strolling with my sister, because mentally it was very difficult to endure being without electricity and water back at home, so we would just go out strolling to relieve this pressure. When we reached Kneza Damjana and Jude Street, which is to the east of town, a street leading to what today is known as the aquarium, to the left, or rather, to the north, there's a high, a very high portion of the town wall. To the right, the bishop's palace, which is also quite tall. At one point, a bullet whizzed past and hit the wall of the palace and ricochetted down on the floor near where we were standing. This was an opportunity for me to find a gleaming piece of the bullet in the gutter just underneath the wall. After that, we continued strolling towards the cathedral - that's to the west. Outside what is the parish office today, there was a scaffolding that had been set up to carry out reparations to the facade. At that time, the metal post that had been hit by bullets rang out. I told my sister: Don't tell me we came here to die. So we just went back home in a hurry. That's how our stroll ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know anyone who was shot by a sniper in November of 1991 in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tonci Kalcic, whose flat had also burnt to the ground. In my neighbourhood - his flat is only ten metres from mine. Later on, he told me that he was hit by a bullet just below the knee. When he came out to walk along a pier, or quay, that we call Porporela, which is at the far end of town, just outside the harbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That's part of the Old Town, but he went strolling along the edge, where obviously he was very much exposed, and those who were standing along the top of the rocks over there could see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware of anyone else being shot, or were you present when anyone else was shot by a sniper within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: There was a group of us, five of us, who probably just chanced to all come together during a stroll, because we could no longer stay at home. We were standing near the aquarium. There a small gate in the wall that leads to the harbour. We were pointing our finger at the silhouettes up there between the peak of Srdj and Zarkovica. Suddenly, one of the men cried because he had been hit in the palm of his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say silhouette, silhouettes of what, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Human silhouettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And this man was injured or shot in the hand. Or when you say he was hit in the hand, was he shot in the hand, or what happened?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously, they could not have thrown a knife from that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was this man within the Old Town when he was shot in the palm of his hand?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: As I said, we were just outside that small gate, the gate in the town wall, near the aquarium, where the pavement of the harbour begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After that shooting incident, or sniping incident, did you and your sister continue to walk around the Old Town in November?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: November. This was in the absence of my sister. The first encounter that I told you about a while ago was with my sister, but this group of people, when these five people were together, this was on a different day, and my sister was not around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But after this incident, did you continue to walk through the Old Town? Did your sister continue to walk through the Old Town after this third shooting incident?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you walked to relieve stress earlier. How did you feel, without power and water and -- limited amount of water? How did you feel? How did you and the others in the Old Town feel?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It felt like we were prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in November, as you walked through the Old Town, did you ever see any Croatian troops in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any mortars, artillery, machine-guns within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any trenches or bunkers in the Old Town for troops?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It would not have been possible to dig any trenches or bunkers within the town itself, because the floor is made of stone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you ever see any soldiers firing out of the Old Town during the month of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us move to December. Were you still living in the Old Town of Dubrovnik in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In that same home on Od Puca Street?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Od Puca number 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let us move to December 6th, 1991. And could you tell us where you were in the early morning hours, about 5.30 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: In bed. My mother, too, in her room, was in bed, on the second floor of the house. My sister and I slept in the same room, because my sister had moved to my room because she was too afraid to stay in her own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did something happen after 5.30 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Regrettably, yes. Something really terrible happened, which later proved to be not only terrible but also tragic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Judges what happened.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: At about 10 to 6.00 in the morning, we were still in bed, and we heard a series of distant explosions. The sound was getting louder, so we assumed that the explosions were getting nearer. We told each other, however, probably it's the same thing as we heard back in November. But the explosions continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: More and more powerful explosions, at which point I told my sister: This is becoming serious. Let's get up and go. I slipped some sort of a bathrobe over my pyjamas and ran over to my mother's room to take her away. When I reached the room, I realised that my mother was no longer in the room. Next I went to a small shelter, some sort of a pantry between my mother's room and the kitchen. We coated the walls of this room with sponge, with quilts and duvets, so that we could have a place to hide comfortably should the need arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were using this room as a type of shelter in your home?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: This room shares a very thick wall with the adjacent -- with the contiguous house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is it in the interior of the house?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: The inside of the house, the second floor, and just above us there was a thick floor of an old Dubrovnik kitchen, made of yellow baked tiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, who was in this shelter or this -- this shelter that you made?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: And then, my sister, who had managed to put her clothes on in the meantime, arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where was your mother?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I found her inside the shelter, and I thought to myself: My God, how is this possible? We were a great deal younger than she was, but she instinctively sensed danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you remain in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, we remained in the shelter until the sounds of these explosions started growing more and more powerful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: As I said, being the restless man that I am, I had to go out and have a look to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "out," did you leave the house or did you stay within the house?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No. In the house. In the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So where did you go to see what was happening?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I went over to the kitchen window facing west, from which you had a very clear view of the hilltop cross on Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I observed constant explosions and thick smoke rising.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: There was a strong easterly wind on that day, and I waited for the wind to disperse, the smokescreen. Once the smoke had lifted, I realised that our cross was gone. The only thing that remained was the vertical bar, but the horizontal arms of the cross had been broken off.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I quickly shut the window and shouted over to my sister and mother, who were taking shelter: Our cross is gone. That's the bad sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you look out the window again?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I went back to the window. It had the wooden shutters. We call them Persijane. I looked outside, looked in the same direction, towards Srdj, and at a distance of about 80 metres, a shell crashed down, and I quickly closed the window again. I ran over to my mother and sister, and I said: It must be our turn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you saw the shell explode at a distance of about 80 metres, what was the area of the city that it exploded in, or what buildings were in that area that the shell exploded?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: This was near the festival headquarters for Dubrovnik Summer Festival, which had burned down, which we later realised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you're back in the shelter area with your mother and sister. What happens? Please tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Another shell exploded overhead. So what I had prophesied had come true. It was our turn, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "exploded overhead", you mean it exploded into your building or it hit your building?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. This was exactly where we had a lavatory in the attic. It was at 10 past 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Does anything happen after that?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Just after that, several minutes later, another shell landed on our house from the west, near the chimney of the house just next to ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen after these shells hit your house that made you realise a shell was hitting your house?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: You realise that there is a great deal of pressure above your head. I said at that time: It's all right. It's all right. Thank God it's not an incendiary shell

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say it hit overhead, was there any debris or anything that fell when those first two shells hit your house?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Mostly the roof caves in, the tiles, and the wooden beams supporting the tiles. You may find this interesting, however. I said: My God, just let it not be an incendiary shell, and my sister said: Shut up, you witch. We didn't have to wait long. At 20 past 7.00, there was another explosion, and you could see a different kind of light, a bluish, strong light. Now, how were we able to see this? Because in the old houses in Dubrovnik, there's not a single window or a single door that shuts tight. Those were no new windows and doors. So through the doors, through the windows, and through the locks, you could see this bluish light.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened after this shell exploded? You see a blue light. What else do you hear or notice?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: At that moment, we crouched, we squatted, to keep our body volume down, and we remained silent. We waited to see if -- and this was a little further to the south than the first shells that fell. We waited to see if anything would move, if we would feel anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you hear or feel?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: And we didn't have to wait for long. We felt that there were things falling up above, that something was rolling down, that something was creaking, that something was breaking. Something was alive up there. My patience ran out, and I said, like a true macho man: You women, you stay put. You stay where you are. I'm going out to see what's going on. When I reached the top of the staircase, first I had to go through the kitchen, then the corridor and the living room, up a flight of stairs, and then I reached the attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: What did I observe? I realised that at the time, where the door meets the door frame, there were tongues of flame coming out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I knew that the room behind the door was on fire. However, having learnt from my earlier experiences when my flat was on fire in Zagreb, I did not open the door, because then oxygen comes into the room and the fire flares up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So tell the Court what you did.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Then I went to the bathroom. We had just built a new bathroom during the Dubrovnik Republic there were no bathrooms, as is generally well known. The bathtub was full of water from the November rains. I took a bucket and tried to douse the flames by throwing water. I was very happy at first. I thought to myself: Hmm, I'm doing fine. When I came out to get another bucket of water, I saw that the flame was growing. I used up seven bucketfuls of water, but I failed to put out the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Next I went back down to the living room, down the flight of stairs. We had two buckets full of water there, which we kept just in case. I took those two buckets back up the stairs. Having reached the top of the stairs, I was surprised to see what I saw. The flame had already devoured one-third of the door, and the door didn't just burn regularly; the flames had eaten the door away, leaving a jagged line, a jagged contour. These jags looked like the devil's teeth. This was in a way magnificent but also a horrifying thing to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was this smoke and fumes?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: You know the saying: Where there's smoke, there's a fire. And vice versa. I still have this horrifying image in my mind. Maybe I'll make a painting out of it one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Then I poured these two bucketfuls of water on to the door, but to no avail. The fire was getting stronger and stronger. I began suffocating from smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So what happened? Did you go back downstairs or ...

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I quickly ran downstairs, to this little room where my mother and sister were, and I told them: We must leave the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you get anyone out of the house, you yourself? Did you help anyone out of the house?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: First I told them: Let's -- everyone go to their respective rooms to take two blankets each. That was an order that had to be complied, without fail. And also, I told them to take all the bare necessities. My mother is a short woman. I took her under her armpits and I had to run down with her, down some 40 stairs to the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did you bring her?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: First I shouted through a small window to my neighbours, asking them: Mrs. Jasna, can you please take care of my mother. And I helped her. I opened the door to the house. I had to go straight, then to the right, then to the left, to our next-door neighbour, Mrs. Obad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, after you left your mother at the Obad house, did you return to your home?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I ran like crazy, and I slammed the door behind me, and I found my sister, and one of the JNA shells exploded to the west of the door, so we were spared the effects of shrapnel. It was a matter of seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me get this straight. You just got back into your house when a shell exploded, or ...

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
