utterances.text: I didn't have time to lock the door to the house. I just slammed the door. I reached my sister, and then the shell exploded, an incendiary shell exploded at the corner of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, where did your sister go?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: My sister was waiting for me. As soon as I took my mother to our neighbour's, I found my sister downstairs. But in addition to the two blankets that I said we must all take, she had a third one, plus a bag, over her shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was in the bag?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I asked her: Why do you have that with you? And she replied: My personal papers. And then I responded: But I don't have anything on me. I took our mother's away and I have nothing on me. So I quickly rushed up to these 40 stairs, to my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you get your documents?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I first peeped through the keyhole to see if there was fire in the room. I quickly opened the door, and then I thought to myself: Where are all my school certificates, my birth certificate, my diplomas? Was I keeping them in the first drawer or in the fourth drawer? And it happened that they were in the third drawer. I took all those folders, stashed them into a bag, and then I took to my mother's room, which was next to mine, and in a cupboard there, she had her small bag where she kept money.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. So you got your money and documents. Did you go back downstairs?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I ran downstairs, and then my sister told me: What about my shoes? And she added: And what about gas cylinder? It's a brand new cylinder full of gas, and it's going to blow up the whole house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So did you run back upstairs to get the slippers and the gas bottle, or cylinder?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I somehow collected my strength. I said to myself: Ivo, you must run upstairs to fetch both your sister's shoes and the gas cylinder. I took those items, and also a small fire extinguisher which works with powder. So I carried all these items downstairs, and when I reached the ground floor, I heard the upper staircase caving in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: These were matters of seconds, or tenths of seconds, by which I avoided being crumbled under this debris. Thankfully, God saved me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you and your sister leave the house and go to the Obad's too?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: My sister was supposed to come out. I told her to put both blankets over her head. Why? Because pieces of roof tiles, hot pieces of planks that supported the tiles were falling down. You can eventually see that on the photographs that I made. My sister went out, but since she was covered with those blankets and carried a bag, she immediately stumbled and fell in front of the door. I shouted at her: Get up on your feet. And then she went to the Obad's, and I was left there alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you find something to put on your head before you left, to protect yourself?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: There's a copper water vessel that was made a long time ago, which we use in Dubrovnik as a reminder of the good old times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you put this copper vessel or copper pot on your head as kind of like a helmet?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the top of a cupboard in my small ground-floor gallery, in which I kept some dry flowers. I threw the flowers outside and I tried to put it on my head, and it fitted perfectly. I also put two blankets over my head and body, and I knelt down on the lower staircase.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: And I said - and I think this is important for me to say now: God, it is up to you whether I'm going to count to 4, 15, or 19 before I can leave the house, because shells were exploding all over the place outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: At one moment in time, I made a decision and went to the Obad's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, just very quickly: While you were at the Obad's house, did you try to do anything to put the fire out?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: The reason we went to their house was because they had the old gustirna as we call it in Dubrovnik, which is a water tank dating back from the time of the old Republic of Dubrovnik. We used that as a source of drinking water. Many people came before this event with a small vessel, and that's how we supplied all the -- the entire neighbourhood with water.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just briefly: What did you do to try and put the fire out from the Obad house?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: In retrospect, it seems to me like some crazy game. We took one litre or two-litre bottles, filled them with water, and we threw them at this huge flame devouring my flat. We had hoped that this could be helpful in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was it helpful?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No. There was no effect. But we simply had to do something and try to save what could be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you able to save any of your paintings?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't have any more strength, because, as I told you, my beautiful art gallery used to be on the ground floor, and it's perished altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But were you able to save any paintings on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Then Mr. Obad told me: We must take this out and bring it to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Another two young gentlemen joined us, and quite incidentally, they're all three called Toni, Tonci, and Antun, which is basically the same name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were these men able to save some of your paintings?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: About 20 paintings were carried over from my gallery to Mr. Obad's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you remain in the Obad house for a while?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We spent the night there and we ate there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you leave the Obad house at any time during the day?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. I put this copper vessel again on my head, and I wrapped these two blankets around me, and I went out of the house to see what was happening and what were the outcome of this terrible shelling. I took a photocamera and I shot the facade of the buildings. I saw a flame coming out from out of the window on the south facade, and that was the window to the room of my sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. You took a picture. Did you have anyone take a picture of you by the building?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: As soon as I took this first photograph, I turned around and I saw a gentleman approaching me quite quickly from the western side. I addressed him. I said: Please, can you make a photo again. And I made this gesture, and this is the picture that was reprinted all around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did something happen right after that photo was taken?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: At that moment, while the second picture was being taken, in the background of the picture, it could be seen that a shell exploded approximately in front of the Greek Orthodox Church, some 70 metres away from the place where I was. Because on the first picture, you don't see this smoke, whereas in the other picture you can see this white smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly: Did you go somewhere after the shell exploded?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We threw ourselves to the street on the right-hand store. We had been some 70 centimetres from the wall. We tried to avoid being hit by any shrapnel. This gentleman was shouting "Keti, Keti," because he had been living at Mrs. Keti's house, and he called to her to open the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If we could be just brief on a lot of these issues, so we can just finish up very quickly. So do you go into this Keti's house and stay for a while?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We both went inside, and shells had been falling all around in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did the firemen eventually arrive during that day, December 6th?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I took this photo exactly at 20 past 3.00 p.m., and the fire brigade arrived at 20 past 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to look at this photograph. Is that you in the picture, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is that the pot you were using as a helmet for protection?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where is your house in that picture? Is that your house with the balcony, to the left of where you're standing?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that was taken, you said, at 3.20 p.m. on December 6th?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, at 3.20 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at the building to your left, there's flames at the top. Whose room is that, if you know? You can see the flames coming out of one of the windows.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. And as I just said, that was my sister's room. And the flame was coming from inside, which means that the entire room had been burned down, because the window was closed, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would move to introduce that photograph at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The photograph will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit P34.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May I continue, or ... Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, just briefly: On December 6th, 1991, did you see any Croatian troops in the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see any mortars, artillery, or even any outgoing fire from the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Not inside the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, on the following day, December 7th, did you go back and visit what was the -- your apartment and the building?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We all went out into the streets, because on the 7th of December, a sort of truce was signed and the shelling ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you return to your apartment on that date?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I had no place to go back. The house was burnt to the ground. But I went around the town and looked at other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were there any other buildings on your street that were destroyed, other than yours?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: This is a well-known fact. Six houses were burnt to the ground, and another three were burnt -- their upper sections were burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's start off with your house. I'd like to show you a photograph with an ERN number 03491268. Do you recognise that photograph, sir? It should be on your screen.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That's the eastern side of the house. And here you can see the balcony. There were two balconies, in fact, on the eastern side. This is the one facing the north-easterly side. And the shell fell beneath the balcony, on the street, and the detonation demolished the stone floor of the balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you -- could you put the picture on that machine to your right. Now, sir, could you please show the floor of the balcony that was damaged, what you were just referring to. Could you point to that, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: The floor was here. This is the front side, upon which this wrought iron fence leaned, and it stretched up to the house wall. And all this part that is missing used to be a stone balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that the witness has just pointed to the floor or the standing area of the balcony, and there's a very large hole. It's just no longer there. And it was, according to his testimony, it was made out of stone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at the next photograph, 03491269. Sir, what is that a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: This is the western part of the house. This wall on the right is in fact the middle wall of the house, the middle supporting wall of the house, because there is an identical area like this on the eastern side as well. There was. The house was 10 by 13 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, this interior portion, there's a line, almost like a triangle, a line along the -- a horizontal line. Is that where the floor was? Higher than that. Yes, right there, the one you just pointed to. What was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the floor of the old kitchen in the attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was there another floor that was there, one storey below?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That's one floor below, and this used to be the floor of our flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did all this damage, two floors of a house gone, did this all occur on December 6th?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It all happened in one day. The house was demolished to the ground. The only thing left are these bare walls that you can see. The western wall, the northern wall, and the middle wall divide -- partitioning the house into two identical portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, could we look at the next photograph, photograph with an ERN number 03491270. Sir, could you tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: In this photograph, you can see the entrance door to the palace.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the palace -- and that's your home at 16 Od Puca Street?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is that the only piece of the door remaining, that piece to the left?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. This piece, I still have this piece. I've kept it. It didn't burn.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what's inside the door or behind the doorway? What's all that pile?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Here you can see, if you look at this wall above the door, there's a circular shape. This was a large fresco that I painted, a ring dance, a folklore ring dance from the surroundings of Dubrovnik. They call it the jig. So a bit further inside, on the adjacent walls, there were murals, or rather, paintings, hung on these walls that those three gentlemen that I spoke about earlier had taken away and saved. If I may just add: On the door jamb, you see a small white tile. This was a ceramic tile, or a plaque, on which I painted a small coat of arms and wrote down the name Kamber, because that was the name of my sister's family.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And would you look at the last picture, 03491271. Now, could you tell us what that photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: First of all, I took this photograph personally, three months later. This is the wall of the house facing west. The photograph was taken from inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What are those two objects, from the middle of the photograph up, those square objects? One is the shape of a U and the one to the left of it's a square.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: This sloping section here was where the roof was, and this window was at the top of the staircase. To the left, you see the zigzag line. That's where the staircase was, and that's the staircase I took to reach the attic and to try to put out the fire. It was from here precisely that I saw, facing east, that the door was burning, that the door that I've talked about was on fire. This window here is where the bathroom was, the lavatory. It was this wide, and that's where we had a small bathroom, with a bathtub to the right, from which I got the seven bucketfuls of water, following which I failed, eventually, to put the fire out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that there are two squares at the top of this photograph. The one to the left, or below the one to the left, the witness just indicated, was a stairway, and the one to the right was the one relating to the bathroom, where he got the buckets of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are these four photographs fair and accurate representations of the way your house looked after it had been shelled and the way it looked on December 7th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. These photographs speak volumes about the atrocity of the attack. This is the state in which the house remained until as late as 1996, when reconstruction began.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to offer these four photographs at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photo with -- bearing ERN number 03491268 is Exhibit P35. The photo bearing ERN number 03491269 is Exhibit P36. The photo bearing ERN number 03491270 is Exhibit P37. And photo bearing ERN number 03491271 is Exhibit P38.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wondered whether that would be a convenient time, Mr. Weiner, or are you very near the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm near the end, but I think it would be a convenient time to take a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Grbic, we're going to have a break now and then resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Mr. Grbic. Now, we just looked at the pictures of the damage to your house. I'd like to ask you, just very briefly: You indicated that the festival headquarters had been struck, or the area above the festival headquarters, and you said you later found out that it had been damaged or destroyed. Is that also referred to as the Festival Palace?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: This palace is in Od Sigurate Street, and to the right of it there's another, bigger palace, which had burned to the ground. To the left is the Festival Palace, of which the attic in the second floor had burned, with the entire archive. People managed to salvage some furniture from the first floor. This you can see on the video footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's from the news footage. All right. On your street - you were living at Od Puca 16 - do you know whether something happened to the house or the building at Od Puca 11?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: On the same street, three more palaces were burned. The nearest to my house is the south-east front of the Maineri Palace, where the Krasovac and Kalcic families lived. This burned to the ground. The next house, next to St. Joseph's church, this was the oldest building of all from the renaissance. It also burned to the ground. Next to the Orthodox Church, there was a very tall building, a three-storey building. The attic and the entire house burned down. South-east of that building, the elementary school building, there was another privately owned palace, a renaissance palace had burned to the ground. On the Stradun, next to the Festival building, that's -- the other side of the little brethren, as I said the attic had burned down and the second floor. The building next to it, the flame had gutted the entire house, leaving only the bare walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, Od Puca number 11, was that one of the houses that had burned on your street, to the ground, that burned to the ground?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the damage to your home, did you lose any artwork and any of your collections?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: As I said, I am an artist, a painter. In addition to my teaching work, I taught in Zagreb for 22 years. I taught art at the applied arts school. In addition to my work as a teacher, I painted. I did paint work, enamel. I did applied arts too, etchings, posters. In that same year, on the 25th of October, I celebrated my 60th birthday, because I had just turned 60. Naturally, if by the age of 60, one failed to establish oneself as a talent, then past the age of 60 then certainly your prospects were not particularly rosy. In addition to my work as a painter, I had a valuable collection of books, more than 2.000 books. I'm not talking about popular literature. This is something I borrowed from other people. This was serious literature from my field of work, from art history, from the history of theatre, metal work, that sort of thing. Everything that came from the field of the visual arts. I collected objects. I had a collection of curios. I owned a model of an old Dubrovnik ship. I also had a private ethnographic collection of old clothes that were used in the surroundings of Dubrovnik ages ago. The Konavle area, Zupa Dubrovacka, the Dubrovnik coastal area to the west and from the island of Mljet. These were very old costumes. I also owned a collection of old instruments, musical instruments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many paintings did you lose?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I believe about 170, 175. I can't say with any degree of precision, but a large number of paintings that were kept in the flat. Many of my etchings were burned. In the attic, I kept three huge wardrobes, 100 by 70 centimetres. The format is usually referred to as B-1. And those wardrobes were filled with my etchings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now -- okay. Now, let me just ask you this, just to clarify the record, and then we'll go into the last section, last few minutes. All those palaces that you indicated were burned to the ground, did all of those burn as a result of the shelling on December 6th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: All of them. As a result of the shelling that took place on the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, after the shelling on that date and the destruction of your home, did your sister ever return to Od Puca 16 to live, to live there?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: She only returned once the house had been repaired. But even the heirs who inherited the house failed to complete the reconstruction because unfortunately she died.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your mother, did she ever return to that home that she lived in since 1970? Did she ever return to Od Puca 16 to live there again?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No. I regret to say, she died in the following year, 1992, prior to which she had been living in an old people's home. So it was from sorrow and from old age that she died, in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you -- you indicated you returned to the home a few years ago. Where did you live for those ten years? Just -- what types of housing you live in over the ten years that you weren't in your home at Od Puca Street?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Most of the refugees lived in hotel facilities. I lived in five different hotels myself, but those were not the hotels that you imagine, that you tend to imagine, luxurious hotels. There was no running water, no electricity, initially. Later, when we did have electricity, it was rationed out, so that there was enough to go around. We washed once a week, and the food was miserable. I stayed in five different hotels, which I can enumerate for you. The first one was the Lapad Hotel. The next one was Imperijal. The third one was the Palace Hotel, in Lapad. The fourth one was the Plakir Hotel, and the last one, finally, was Vis-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Grbic, good afternoon. My name is Vladimir Petrovic. I'm an attorney at law from Belgrade and I represent General Strugar before this Tribunal. I will ask you several questions in connection with your testimony before this Court today. First of all, can you please tell me whether at any point in time you gave a statement to the investigators of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember specifically when and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: In September 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend is drawing my attention to the fact that since we speak the same language, we should pause between question and answer, because the proceedings are being interpreted. When did you give this statement, and to whom? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: In Dubrovnik, in Lapad, at the Kompas Hotel. I spoke to Mr. Mohammad Arshad, I think that's what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you answer his questions on that issue?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. Arshad what happened in October, November, and December 1991 to the best of your knowledge and recollection at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: He wrote this down. Did you read it before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It was written in English. You know that I don't understand English, so the interpreter just read the statement back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What the interpreter read back to you, did that accurately reflect your words to Mr. Arshad, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say yes, for the most part. Did you perhaps point out certain discrepancies or inaccuracies to Mr. Arshad at the time, imprecisions in the statement, once it was read back to you by the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I could only ascertain this now, when I saw it in writing, the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But if I understand you correctly, back in 2000, on that occasion when you were interviewed, your statement was read back to you and there were no objections on your part.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult to make any objections to an oral statement. As you know, the speech flows. If I had had a written statement before me, I would have been in a better place to go through it and analyse the text itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So was it read back to you or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was read back to me, but in a leisurely way. I could not obtain a copy of the statement in writing. Purportedly, that's at least what I was told, this was not the usual practice at the Tribunal. We signed it, and it was only now that I had occasion to see certain inaccuracies and inconsistencies in the written statement, which at the time I could not correct, because that was oral communication, so speech tends to flow and you can't interrupt people all the time. Had I had a written copy of the statement back then, I would have had the chance to go back to certain things and mistakes. Because as you are no doubt well aware, even a single comma can change the meaning of an entire sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This means that you signed the statement, although even at the time you realised that there were inaccuracies in the statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anything at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Or rather, you heard.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It was read back to me so fast that I didn't have a chance to realise that there were shortcomings in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the end of the statement, was a caution read out to you, to the witness, saying that the statement is to the best of your knowledge and recollection, on the one hand; and on the other, that the statement can be used in proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for persons accused of committing crimes in the former Yugoslavia, which means that this has potentially far-reaching legal consequences?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That's precisely why the investigation was carried out. That was the aim, the original objective of the investigation. But all of us who provided statements expected that if we signed anything, that we would eventually be given a copy of the document we signed, as is the established practice with most law courts. My lawyer would have been entitled to claim a copy of the statement. Unfortunately, none of my friends and fellow victims in Dubrovnik were ever given copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you set eyes on the statement for the first time?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Recently, when I arrived in The Hague. In writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was it like? Were there several people who were giving statements being interviewed at the same time? How were you summoned there? How was the whole thing organised, technically?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It was always individual, individual interviews were conducted with the investigator present and an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who had summoned you to the Kompas Hotel where you gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That's not what I was staying at the time. I was staying at the Vis-2 Hotel and that's where Mr. Arshad interviewed other refugees too. So one day he left a message for me saying that he would wait for me, he'd be waiting at the Kompas, and the distance between the two hotel, the one where I was staying and where I was interviewed was perhaps 500 metres, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you asked Mr. Arshad for a copy of the statement, but he failed to produce one?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: He said that this was not usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I would like to move on to something different now, another issue that you raise in your statement. Wherever possible, please try to keep your answers brief, obviously. If you can't, your answers will be lengthy. But if you can keep them short, please do so. In your statement, page 1, in fact, of your statement, in the last passage, you say the following: "The history of this region from the 19th century onwards shows that the Serbs had the tendency to dominate other ethnic groups." What exactly did you mean by that? How was this reflected? How was this apparent? Why was it important to include that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Because history teaches us. History is a teacher. We are able to draw many conclusions from the course of history. This was something that we were aware of. But I think even now in schools in Serbia, children are taught that the Renaissance and Baroque literature of Dubrovnik is Serbian literature, which is a blatant untruth. Even if you just look at that example of arbitrariness, this clearly reflects a desire to dominate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the nineteenth century. What is the importance of pointing out the Serb desire to dominate back in the nineteenth century? How does that affect something that happened at the end of the twentieth century?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Because it was the same thing earlier. I'm just trying to point out that this in fact never stopped, that this desire to dominate never stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you recognise this desire to dominate at the time relevant to our conversation?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I used the nineteenth century.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about both the 19th and the twentieth century?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Back in the nineteenth century, the population of Dubrovnik was predominantly Catholic. There wasn't a single church in Dubrovnik that wasn't a Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. Your Honour, within the statement, there are -- let me count. One, two, three, possibly four paragraphs, some of them long, concerning a whole history of the Dubrovnik area, going back to the nineteenth century. They take it from the nineteenth century, into the twentieth century, to post World War II, on to the current situation. I didn't introduce any of that during the Prosecution's examination-in-chief because we had a historian come and testify. This man discussed it, but he is not a historian. He's not qualified as a historian, although he's a noted artist. And we didn't bring that up. As a result, I'd argue that it's not relevant to this proceeding, unless they can come up with some way to tie the nineteenth century history --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two things to point out. I'll just dwell on this very briefly, on this issue of history. Secondly, if you read the statement of this witness, the source, the roots of the 1991 conflict, in the opinion of this witness, are to be found in something that dates far back in history. I'll dwell on this very briefly, because we're talking about an armed conflict. But this witness is trying to point out the roots, the sources of this conflict. I'm not spending too much time on this, but I believe that some light should be shed on this issue, because in many ways this has been raised by the OTP during the pre-trial stage and even now, and also, this was something we heard from another witness. So obviously, this is something that keeps cropping up in the positions put forward by the OTP. So therefore I believe it is necessary to discuss this in Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You realise, Mr. Petrovic, that while it was in a statement that you have, it was not led in evidence, so this witness hasn't given any evidence about the matter and the Chamber has not heard anything from this witness about the history. It's not immediately apparent to me what will be relevant about that history. If you can point out where it will be directly relevant to your case, it will be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I'd just like to add two questions, and if by then this is not clarified, we can move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Fine. Yes, do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Going back to your statement, what does the following statement mean: "Serbian nationalistic poets swamped Dubrovnik"?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: This was a misinterpretation, so now we've got that corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So how should it be now, this sentence? How should it read?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It should read as follows: Some poets from Dubrovnik, such as the Pucic brothers and Nikola Ban [phoen], who were pro-Serbian, wrote certain poems which could again be heard in 1991. You can see that on the video footage of the man playing the Gusle, a traditional instrument, singing: On the top of Srdj, the fairy is singing. Long live Serbian Dubrovnik. These lines were actually written by Nikola Ban in mid-19th century. That's precisely how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that on the land belonging to the Gundulic family, an Orthodox church was built around which political activity of the local Serbs centred. Why do you have a problem with an Orthodox church in a cosmopolitan tradition, a cosmopolitan town? Why is a Serb poet something to be surprised at?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I'm saying a pro-Serbian poet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Pro-Serbian or Serbian?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not the same thing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What's your problem with that?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you how it was. Back in the nineteenth century, the Dubrovnik nobility became poor and rich merchants from the hinterland came over and bought their houses off the Dubrovnik nobility on a massive scale, which is recounted by Vojnovic in his Dubrovnik trilogy. Vaso turned the Tunisici [phoen] house into a warehouse where salt was kept. The old nobility was obviously just short of dying from heart break. So this was the general trajectory, the general course the events took. So the church was only built in the second half of the nineteenth century, plumb in the middle of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you mind a Serbian church being there in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No, I don't mind. As a matter of principle, I don't mind any place of worship, as a matter of principle. But it was requested explicitly that the church be built at the very centre of town, at the geometrical centre point, so this is usurping space inside the town, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you think this is a blemish on the town's face?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: It was not exactly built according to the rules set out by earlier buildings in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My last question concerning this: Who rules Dubrovnik at the time the Serbian church was built? Was it a Serbian ruler? Was it Yugoslavia? Who was in charge? Who were the rulers at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I said the nobility had become poor and then the rich merchants came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just to keep this brief: What was the estate at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Austro-Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we look at your statement, another fact that I find very interesting is something that relates to the most recent events. You say: "Following the death of President Tito, the ethnic factor predominated, became predominant again and Serbs were now controlling all the key posts in non-Serb areas." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Well, this means, and that is the truth itself, is that in the Yugoslav army, most of the leading officers in the army were Serbs. I think that's no secret. Or is it? It's clear, if you look at this last war and the attack on Dubrovnik, what songs were sung.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, let's not start talking about songs. Just try to keep to my questions. If you can, please answer my questions. If not, please make that clear and say you can't. You say that all the most important positions in the army and in the financial sector were in the hands of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry to object again, but once again we're delving into areas not covered in direct examination. Now, I know cross-examination can delve into issues that are not covered in direct examination or examination-in-chief. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With leave of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With leave of the Tribunal. However, in this situation again, number one, they are questioning this witness as a historical expert. We did not -- we did not question this witness in those areas because he is not a historical witness. And if this Court would like to take judicial notice, if you want to look at the Talic decision and other decisions of this Tribunal, it is clear that what this witness had just said was stated in the Talic decision about the changes that occurred in the JNA, where it did in fact become a Serbian army. But that's beside the point. That information came from military people and experts that testified. This person is not a historical expert, and as a result, this area is irrelevant. That's number one. Number two, even, even if the Court wanted to hear such testimony, this person's opinion as to the causes of the war and the events that led up to the war, once again, are not admissible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Now, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it goes without saying that the Chamber will not base its final opinion on what this witness says. However, what this witness has to say in relation to these specific issues has a bearing on his entire view of how events unfolded, and this has a bearing on this indictment. If someone puts forward certain positions, certain kinds of prejudice, if someone's memory is partial, at best, now, this must be heard, and that's what I'm trying to draw everyone's attention to. I don't mean to use this to ascertain what happened after Tito died but I want to know why, in the statement of this witness, with great vehemence there is great focus on a problem which purportedly exist in Dubrovnik and has to do with Serbs. What I want to get at is why all things Serbian seem to be a problem for this witness, which comes across with great clarity, if you look at his statement. Because this is a key issue for his later interpretation of what happened. I am not trying to verify historical facts through the testimony of Mr. Grbic. I will just dwell on this very briefly, but I think it matters. I think it's material to the testimony of this particular witness. This has nothing to do with the overall historical interpretation of certain events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you realise that again I suspect you are concentrating on matters which are not in evidence. You seem to be looking at the statement, which the members of the Chamber don't have and which are not in evidence, and you are saying: Well, there are things in that that concern you and you want to examine on. What we have heard from Mr. Grbic is very largely a factual description of damage and loss in the Old Town of Dubrovnik. That's the evidence which we have from the witness. It would normally be unusual for you to broaden his evidence in cross-examination. There would need to be some good reason why that should be allowed to occur. Now, the most I can make from what you've put against that background is that you think that this cross-examination will go to the credit, the credibility of aspects of the evidence that has been given by Mr. Grbic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the first thing you said, yes, in addition to other reasons which I have tried to point out, because the problem we are facing now is the following, if I may be allowed to use these several minutes to clarify this. We have in front of us a person who witnessed these events that are material to the indictment. However, what we see happening now is that this witness gave a statement, and Mr. Weiner took him through his testimony, omitting certain key aspects of our case. But key aspects of our case have been referred to in this witness's statement. However, during the examination-in-chief, they have simply been omitted. And I'm not talking about the historical part now, because that I fully accept. But everything else is key to our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And very soon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, if I could invite you to indicate what it is that is important to your case that you want to explore with Mr. Grbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try. First of all, unfortunately, I see that we are having this conversation in the presence of Mr. Grbic, which may affect further course of his testimony. First of all, we have the genesis of armed conflict and participants in this armed conflict, not from a historical point of view, but rather, those who were directly or indirectly involved in this armed conflict. Secondly, how damage occurred and what the circumstances were. The question of armed conflict that was there in the area where only a partial view, at best, is being offered of it. If we only talk about the examination-in-chief and leave everything else aside for the time being, events are being shown from one side, from one of their aspect only, and it seems to be the case that nothing else exists, whereas this witness does make reference to other things in his statement, clearly. Yet my learned friend and colleague never deigns to ask him, What is it that's happening on Srdj but rather they talk about silhouettes and the shelling of the Old Town. But what is the general framework in which all these individual things happen? Maybe the witness knows. Maybe he has no familiarity with this, but it's up to me, it's my duty to ask, to find out whether he knows or not. Mr. Weiner seems to be conveniently skipping over these details in his own examination, but for us there is no reason to avoid these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, let me indicate, Mr. Petrovic, that I have a fairly clear appreciation of why Mr. Weiner is omitting these matters. That is because he is confining and limiting the Prosecution case, and it's not apparent to me that he's doing so to avoid bringing out matters that are to the advantage of your case. That's why I asked you to indicate what it was that you saw was being omitted that was part of your case. To me, what Mr. Weiner is doing is merely limiting out, omitting irrelevant material, none of which will be part of the Prosecution case against your client. If there is in the material that's omitted something that is important to your case, well, then obviously it should be dealt with, and you're free to do that. But at the moment, I haven't grasped exactly what it is, except that you clearly indicated you wanted to explore with Mr. Grbic the question of the damage. Quite clearly, you should be free to do that. What isn't clear to me, for example, is what is the relevance of the history that you were briefly exploring, that goes back perhaps a century or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the statement and the attitudes of the witness are biased. What I wish to achieve through my questioning is to point out to this narrow-mindedness and partiality. That was my objective. And speaking about distant history, I fully agree with you that this is irrelevant, and I'm going to omit this now and in the future, because you think that this is something inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because, Mr. Petrovic, it's not been shown to me how it is relevant, and that's why I've made those comments. But I applaud what you're proposing to do, and if you want to deal with the question of the credibility of the witness, you may ask questions that are relevant to that as well. Now, I see you still on your feet, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was just going to comment that jus in bello is not jus ad bellum that what happened that he's a witness to is one thing. The basis and the historical reasons for it is another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've dealt with that, and it's out of the scene. And I hope I've understood what you have been doing correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petrovic, if you'd like to carry on with your examination, omitting the history that doesn't seem to have any direct relevance, and dealing with the other matters, I think that's where we can go from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned, when you referred to the year 1991, that you started to feel tensions and uncertainty and that you realised that something was wrong. When was exactly that you started feeling like that in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We started feeling like that already when the so-called log revolution was launched in the Krajina in Croatia. That means that the Serbs in Croatia started obstructing roads and other communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for them doing that?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Because on the referendum, they declared a part of Croatia as the Serbian Krajina, not to mention that what we heard later on about what was happening in Vukovar and around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: When did you find out that something was going on in the area of Konavle?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: As soon as the first refugees arrived from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Give me the time framework.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: In early October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true what you say in your statement, at the end of September 1991, the JNA started operations in Konavle?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: They imposed a sea blockade --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be brief. Tell me: Is it correct that in September 1991 the JNA start what you dubbed operations in Primorje and Konavle?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I didn't say in Primorje and Konavle. I said that there was a sea blockade. We could see ships on the horizon and we could not go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you and read what is written in the B/C/S translation, fourth paragraph: "In September 1991, we came to know that the JNA had started its operation in Konavle and Primorje area, which are areas on the south and north-east of Dubrovnik respectively."

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We know that it all happened in early October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, were there any members of the Croatian army in Konavle?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know was there any conflict in Konavle in September and October 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That's far away from the town of Dubrovnik, so the only information we had was from the media. Otherwise, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you want to know why those refugees were pouring in and what was going on?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the hotels were packed with refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please concentrate on my question. My question was: Did you want to find out, did you ask yourself why those people were coming in?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Because their houses were burnt. All -- the whole villages were -- in Konavle were burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question. Were there two sides there shooting at each other, or you don't know, or it wasn't like that?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Lokrum. Can you tell this Chamber how far is Lokrum from the old city, from the Old Town? Several hundred metres? How many?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: At the closest part of the island, it's 700 metres from the city walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that somebody stopped you on your way to Lokrum. Who stopped you?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: The members of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: In late September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did they stop you?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: They told us that we had to go back home because the sea was under the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So where were those members of the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: They were in the harbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you boarded a boat, you arrived at Lokrum, and you were immediately sent back?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were immediately sent back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How come that you managed to reach Lokrum if the sea was under the blockade?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Because nobody told us what the situation was at the town harbour. We learned about that only after we had arrived, and due to that, we were even more surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That means that the city harbour was not under the blockade?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: The army ships were far away from the shore.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But nobody prevented you from sailing outside the town harbour and arriving at the Lokrum harbour?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yeah. No. At that moment, no, but apparently, in the meantime, they were instructed to return any boat or small boat from the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You sailed across the sea and went to the Lokrum -- went to Lokrum?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We had to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Once you arrived at Lokrum, what was the reason for them preventing you to disembark?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: In that case, we would become prisoners on the island of Lokrum, if we had been prevented from returning back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That means that the civilian protection stopped you from setting foot on Lokrum at all?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Whose civilian protection was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Those were citizens, members of local communes, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that they had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you know, then, that they were civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: They were all dressed in civilian clothes, just like I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that anyone dressed in civilian clothes was a member of the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yeah. In a certain manner -- way of speaking, you could say that all citizens protected their town from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if they had no weapons, no uniforms, nor any insignia that will differentiate them from you, why did you obey them?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Because we knew those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You knew who members of the Dubrovnik civilian protection were?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who the Dubrovnik policemen were?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: There was not a single policeman on Lokrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please answer my question. Were you familiar with the policemen of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Not personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear that the Croatian army held positions on Lokrum?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did it perhaps occur to you that you were not allowed to disembark on Lokrum particularly for that reason, that there were military installations there?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No. We just accepted their answers that there were ships on the horizon, the siege was proclaimed, and they told us that we must go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You described in detail that events -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would these civilians -- would have prevented you if you still insisted on remaining on the island?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We didn't have any -- there was no need for us to provoke any conflicts with them. We had to obey them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were they authorised to prevent you?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: We are a peaceful people, and there was no need to have any clash with them. We realised what the situation was. We saw those ships off-shore and we returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did the Croatian defenders take hold of Srdj?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I can't say precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were they on Srdj on the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were they there on the 15th of October?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many of them there were?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, you say in your statement: "The Croatian defenders who, as far as I know, numbered nine, and they tried to defend Dubrovnik from Srdj"?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That's what I learned only later, after all the atrocities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you understand my questions or am I not being accurate enough? My question was: What can you tell us about this today, to this Chamber? I asked you how many men were on Srdj. You answered that you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: You asked me how many of them were in October and November, and I said I didn't know. And what I stated in my statement was the information that I acquired only later, after the war, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So speaking today, how many of those men were in Srdj at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't know how many of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You don't understand me. What can you tell us today about how many Croatian soldiers were on Srdj in October and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Just what I heard, that there had been nine of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What else did you hear about those nine men?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know all these nine men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. I just asked you: What did you hear about those men, if anything?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I heard that they were very brave and courageous.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about their bravery?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That they were just a few of them and that they created an impression that there were much more men there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear how they managed to create such an impression?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Apparently they prevented the capture of this most important feature, and that is the Srdj peak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Did you hear how they managed to create such an impression that their numbers were much larger?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Only the enemy knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat my question again. Have you heard how they managed to create an impression that there were much more of them there?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any stories about their bravery?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: These stories are still being told up to this date, but in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What are the stories being told nowadays?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That they should be highly commended for their bravery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you say in your statement as follows: "Volunteers from the town took them food and brought back the wounded and told stories about their bravery"? Does that mean that you heard about none of these?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I heard only later that down this slope, they carried the wounded downwards, and I really think this is highly commendable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you about that. I'm asking you about the stories about their bravery. Tell me what these stories were, or tell me that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: That the Serbian forces failed to reach the peak of Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how those people were armed?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, had they any weapons at all?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were they perhaps unarmed but brave?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm a civilian. I was not a member of any military formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself see these Croatian defenders from your window?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you see from your window the Imperial Fortress on the Srdj mountain, or hill?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Had you ever noticed any individuals in the Imperial Fortress at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that there were any firing or shooting coming from the Imperial Fortress in November and December?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I wonder where you're positioned now. Are you near the end of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, then we will need to adjourn for the day, then, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Grbic. We must ask you to return again tomorrow to finish. The Chamber would indicate for counsel that we've had a chance to consider the submissions concerning the witness General Pringle. The Chamber is of the view that his evidence is relevant and should be received. Many of the matters that were raised in the Defence submissions appear to have some force, but they are relevant to the weight and the force of the evidence rather than the question of its admissibility, is the way we see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the Chamber adjourns and perhaps rather than keep the witness if I could ask for two minutes of housekeeping time. Something has been raised by the witness unit which I wanted the Chamber to be aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Grbic, thank you very much for today. If we could ask you to leave now and we will see you again tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is it possible to have a private session, or is it necessary to stay in public for a moment? Just simply because of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see -- I don't appreciate why there is a need to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Only because I wanted to relay -- I have not had a chance to meet yet, but I have been given a heads up about some concerns and I -- rather than commit to a position, I just wanted to let the Chamber know that there is a discussion that will be had this afternoon concerning, as I understand it, the number of witnesses coming and having to go back because of various matters. And it is of course a concern for the unit. I'm fine with remaining in open, but I think it's something that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we'll remain in open.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's fine. I have not yet had an opportunity to have contact -- you know, direct contact yet with the director of the unit, but I believe that one of the issues, from what I've been told by our liaison person is the numbers of people we have to schedule in order to accommodate the proposed finish date and then the reality, of course, being that some of these people have to be here for more than three days, which is not according to rules without taking the stand. In order to accommodate the requirement for an advance schedule for notice, we have to do one thing, and then the reality of course becomes another. I will inform the Chamber if I may through the legal officer of what discussions come up, but I think it's something that will probably not be a one-time concern. And I can only leave it at that, since I've not yet had the meeting but I'm concerned enough to let you know it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will await developments, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of January, 2004 at 9.00.
